segs.text: What if America had never built its railroads?
In eighteen thirty, the United States had twenty three miles of railroad. By eighteen ninety, about one hundred sixty thousand. By nineteen sixteen, the peak: about a quarter of a million miles.
Today, freight railroads still carry about forty percent of America's long distance freight, measured in ton miles. That is more than any other way of moving goods.
And a train is efficient. The railroads report that one ton of freight travels nearly five hundred miles on a single gallon of fuel. They estimate that is three to four times better than a truck.

So without railroads, would the country have stalled? In nineteen sixty four, economist Robert Fogel argued: not by much. He compared eighteen ninety with a country of rivers, canals, and wagons. For farm freight, he put the savings from railroads at no more than two point seven percent of national output. He shared the Nobel Prize in economics in nineteen ninety three.

The debate did not end there. Critics said Fogel compared railroads to an economy that never existed. In twenty sixteen, economists Donaldson and Hornbeck estimated that without railroads, American farmland in eighteen ninety would have been worth about sixty percent less. That measures land value, not output, so the numbers do not directly compare. Economists still argue.

Railroads also changed the clock. Before November eighteenth, eighteen eighty three, every town kept its own sun time. That day, the railroads switched to standard time zones. People called it the Day of Two Noons. Congress made it law in nineteen eighteen.

So what if trains stopped today? About forty percent of long distance freight would have to move onto other modes, mostly trucks, which use roughly three to four times the fuel for each ton. The railroads are quiet. But a lot rides on them.
